note_claims.claim: Routine lithium monitoring review for bipolar affective disorder.
Patient reports stable mood and good energy.
Wife reports reduced sleep (about 5 hours) and increased talkativeness and new projects over the last week, which preceded his previous relapse.
Patient denies racing thoughts or overspending.
Patient has no missed lithium doses.
Patient took naproxen (his brother's) for back pain for 3–4 days last week, initially recalled as ibuprofen.
Patient reports diarrhoea and unsteadiness; no vomiting or confusion.
Patient has a long-standing fine tremor, unchanged.
Fine tremor of both hands, unchanged.
Gait is steady.
Lithium level today is 0.7 mmol/L (12-hour post-dose), which is in range.
eGFR is 74, the same as before.
Thyroid function and calcium are normal.
Possible early signs of hypomanic relapse reported by wife.
Continue Priadel 800 mg at night.
Repeat lithium level in 3 months.
Avoid NSAIDs; paracetamol is fine for back pain.
Inform community mental health team.
Keep a sleep diary; contact care coordinator if under 5 hours' sleep for two consecutive nights.
If vomiting, diarrhoea, coarse tremor, unsteadiness or confusion: stop lithium and seek an urgent lithium level or attend A&E.
Avoid dehydration, especially in hot weather.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician greeted Mr Fairweather-Okoro and his wife Adaeze.
Adaeze confirmed she was present.
Relative greeted the clinician.
Clinician asked if it was okay for Adaeze to stay.
Adaeze confirmed she was okay with staying.
Clinician initiated the routine lithium review.
Patient reports mood has been steady and work is going well.
Clinician asked about sleep.
Patient reported fine sleep.
Relative reported the patient has been sleeping less this last week (five hours, maybe) and has been talking a lot more and starting lots of projects, which started last time.
Patient reports feeling well and having loads of energy.
Clinician asked if the patient was having any racing thoughts or spending more money than usual.
Patient denied racing thoughts or overspending.
Clinician asked if the patient was on Priadel, 800 milligrams at night.
Patient confirmed he is on Priadel, 800 milligrams at night.
Clinician asked about missed doses.
Patient confirmed he has never missed a dose.
Clinician asked about other recent medicines, including those from the chemist.
Patient initially recalled taking ibuprofen, but corrected himself to naproxen, which his brother gave him for his back.
Patient stated he took the naproxen for three or four days.
Patient denied having any diarrhoea or vomiting.
Patient denied feeling unsteady on his feet or muddled.
Patient reported no change in his fine tremor, stating it is the same little shake he has always had.
Patient confirmed he drinks plenty of fluids, having a big water bottle at work.
Patient confirmed he has no other medicines and no allergies.
Clinician reviewed blood tests: lithium level last month was 0.7 mmol/L (12-hour post-dose), eGFR is 74 (stable), and thyroid and calcium are normal.
Clinician examined the patient's hands and noted a fine tremor in both hands, the same as before, and confirmed he was walking steadily.
Clinician planned to recheck the lithium level in one week, 12 hours after the evening dose, and then return to every three months.
Clinician advised the patient not to take ibuprofen or naproxen, suggesting paracetamol for back pain.

Clinician planned to inform the community mental health team, ask the patient to keep a sleep diary, and instruct him to contact his care coordinator or the clinic if he sleeps less than five hours for two nights running.

Clinician instructed the patient to continue Priadel at the same dose and provided safety-netting advice: if he gets vomiting, diarrhoea, a coarse shaking, unsteadiness or confusion, he should stop the lithium and seek an urgent lithium level or go to A&E.
Clinician advised the patient to try not to get dehydrated, especially in hot weather.

findings.rationale: The note incorrectly states the patient reports diarrhoea and unsteadiness, when the transcript shows the patient denied these symptoms.
